bp: Many real systems are networks whose important parts are not obvious from size alone. In a citation network, a small group of papers may hold together a field because many later papers depend on them. In a protein interaction network, a group of genes may matter for diagnosis because their relationships and biological attributes jointly signal disease. The paper asks how to find an influential group of nodes in an attributed graph, meaning a network where each node has its own descriptive facts as well as links to other nodes. Older influence maximization methods mostly looked at the connection pattern: who points to whom, who reaches many others, or who sits on important paths. GGUN starts from a broader need. If influence comes from both position in the network and node attributes, then the search for important groups should listen to both sources at once, and should explain why a learned graph model treats a group as important.
wh: The hard part is that group influence is not just individual importance added up. A node can matter because of its attributes, because of its links, or because it completes a useful pattern with other nodes. A citation paper may be influential because it is widely cited, but also because its topic, venue, or method connects otherwise separate communities. A gene may matter because its measured properties and its interaction partners jointly reveal disease relevance. If a method uses only graph structure, it ignores the extra knowledge stored on nodes. If it uses only attributes, it loses the relational clue that nearby or connected nodes can support one another. The search space is also difficult: choosing the best group from many nodes is a combinatorial problem, meaning each possible subset is a separate candidate. Trying every group quickly becomes infeasible. GGUN therefore has to combine structure and attributes while avoiding an exhaustive search over all possible node groups.
naive: A smart beginner might rank nodes with a familiar network score, take the top few, and call them the influential group. That works only if influence is mostly about link position. The abstract says previous approaches often manipulated graph structure and neglected node attributes, so this beginner solution can miss nodes whose descriptive features carry essential knowledge. Another beginner might train a graph neural network, a model that mixes node information through links, then inspect the largest learned weights. That also breaks because graph groups are discrete objects: a node is either chosen or not chosen. Usual feature-importance tools from neural networks do not directly solve the problem of selecting a group of connected nodes under a group-size constraint.
ap: GGUN's central move is to treat influential-group search as an explanation problem. First, it lets a graph neural network read the whole attributed graph, so node attributes and graph structure are fused through its layers. In plain terms, each node updates its internal description using its own facts and evidence arriving from neighbors. Then GGUN asks a perturbation question: if we disturb or remove candidate nodes, how much does the model's understanding of the graph change? The influential group is the set whose perturbation causes the most meaningful damage to the model's behavior. This turns influence from a hand-written centrality rule into a measured dependency: important nodes are those the learned graph model cannot easily do without. Because exact group selection is infeasible, the paper relaxes the discrete group-picking problem into an easier mathematical form and reports a performance guarantee for the efficient solution.
mech: The mechanism begins with an attributed graph. The inputs are nodes, links among nodes, and attributes attached to each node, such as paper information in a citation network or gene-related measurements in a protein interaction network. A graph neural network processes this input in layers. At each layer, a node keeps some of its own current description and receives messages from linked nodes; after several layers, the model has a description shaped by both local attributes and surrounding structure. GGUN then uses perturbation-based explanation. Perturbation means deliberately changing part of the input and watching how the model response changes. Candidate node groups are treated as parts that may be masked, weakened, or otherwise disturbed. If changing a group greatly alters the model's output or internal understanding, that group receives high importance. The difficult step is choosing the best group. There are too many possible groups to enumerate, so the paper formulates the choice as combinatorial optimization: define a score for a selected group, then search for the group with the best score under selection constraints. Because the direct version is infeasible, GGUN relaxes it, replacing the hard yes-or-no selection with a smoother version that can be solved efficiently. The output is an identified influential node group, along with explanation-style evidence for why those nodes mattered.
math: The first mathematical idea is graph reasoning. The graph is a map: nodes are papers, genes, or other entities; links say which entities are related; attributes are the facts stored at each node. A graph neural network is a repeated averaging-and-transforming procedure over that map. It lets evidence travel across links, while still keeping node-specific facts. This fits the paper because influence in an attributed graph may live in the interaction between what a node is and where it sits. The second idea is perturbation-based importance. Instead of guessing importance from appearance, the method changes a part of the input and measures the resulting damage. The ordinary principle is dependency: if the answer changes when a group is disturbed, the model depended on that group. The third idea is combinatorial optimization, which means choosing a subset from many possible subsets according to a score. The exact search is hard because group choices multiply rapidly as the graph grows. Relaxation is the fourth idea: replace an all-or-nothing selection with a softer problem that is easier to compute, then convert it back into a usable group. The tradeoff is exactness versus feasibility: a direct search is faithful but too costly, while a relaxed search is practical and needs a guarantee to justify the shortcut.
dots: This paper sits inside the conference's graph-learning thread because it treats connected structure as evidence rather than background decoration. It is especially close to work on graph explanations: the repo includes a WSDM 2026 tutorial on GNN explainers that describes influential nodes, edges, subgraphs, and features as ways to make graph model behavior understandable. GGUN uses that same explanatory instinct, but turns it toward influence maximization rather than only explaining a final classification. It also connects to influence-maximization work such as DynaFLUX in the social-networks-influence family file, where the shared question is how to choose spreaders or important actors when simple topology is unavailable, hidden, or incomplete. GGUN's surface setting is different because it explicitly has both links and node attributes. The broader recurring ideas are ranking, graph reasoning, and optimization: rank candidate node groups, let evidence move through links, and solve a constrained selection problem without trying every subset.
ww: GGUN should improve over the naive structure-only approach because it asks the graph model to learn from the same two sources that define the real object: links and attributes. If a citation-network node is important partly because of its topic, or a protein node is important partly because of its biological measurements, a method that ignores attributes throws away evidence before scoring influence. GGUN also improves over hand-written centrality rules because the score is tied to model dependency. The perturbation test asks a concrete counterfactual question: what happens to the learned graph understanding when this group is changed? A truly influential group should create a larger change than a decorative group, because many predictions or internal descriptions leaned on it. The relaxation step matters for a different reason: it keeps the method usable. The best exact subset may be impossible to find by brute force, so an efficient relaxed solution gives a practical path while the reported guarantee limits how much trust is being placed in an approximation.
po: The payoff is a way to identify influential node groups in attributed graphs while explaining why those groups matter. The abstract names citation networks and protein-protein interaction networks as examples, so the capability is useful when people need to collect important proceedings or identify essential genes for diagnosis. The paper reports evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, where GGUN outperforms baselines on quantitative metrics and human-intelligible analysis. The important practical gain is not only a higher score; it is a selection method that can use both graph structure and node attributes and can present influence as model-supported evidence rather than as a bare network statistic.
limits: The claims depend on the graph neural network learning a useful view of the graph. If the model has learned spurious correlations, perturbation may highlight nodes the model relies on, not nodes that are truly important in the world. The approach also assumes node attributes contain additional knowledge worth using; in noisy or misleading attribute sets, fusing attributes with structure can hurt. The abstract says the relaxed optimization has a performance guarantee, but it does not give the conditions in this input, so the exact guarantee cannot be inspected here. Human-intelligible analysis is reported, but the abstract does not prove that domain experts would agree in every citation or biological setting.
